title: Chef Ranveer Brar Says 80 Percent of Coriander's Flavor Lives in the Stems Most Cooks Throw Away
excerpt: The celebrity chef breaks down when to use stems versus leaves, and why chopping coriander even an hour early costs you a fifth of its aroma.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • 80% of coriander's flavor is in the stems, not the leaves.
  • Stems are ideal for slow-cooked dishes; leaves for garnishing.
  • Cutting coriander leaves an hour early loses 20% of aroma.
  • Proper storage can extend coriander's freshness for days.

Insights from Chef Ranveer Brar
  • Chef Ranveer Brar says 80 percent of coriander's taste is concentrated in the stems, with only 20 percent in the leaves — making stem disposal a significant waste of flavor.
  • Stems deliver a strong, woody flavor suited to slow-cooked dishes, while leaves provide floral notes best added at the end of cooking or as garnish.
  • Cutting coriander leaves even an hour before use costs roughly 20 percent of their volatile top notes, according to Brar.
  • Proper storage — keeping coriander dry, refrigerating in ziplock bags with a moist tissue, and reviving with chilled (not iced) water — can extend its freshness for days.

In most Indian kitchens, coriander stems get stripped and discarded before the leaves are chopped for garnish. Celebrity chef Ranveer Brar wants that to stop. In a social media video that has resonated widely with home cooks, Brar declared: "Jo dhaniya ki dandi fekta hai na, woh mera kabhi dost nahi ho sakta" — anyone who throws away coriander stems can never be his friend.

The 80-20 Split

The core of Brar's argument is a number: 80 percent of coriander's flavor sits in the stems, with only 20 percent in the leaves. That does not mean the leaves are decorative. They carry a distinctly different character — floral and bright — while the stems are woody and deep. The mistake most cooks make is treating the entire plant as a single ingredient rather than two.

In an interview with Slurrp, Brar described coriander as "a typical root-to-fruit ingredient." The roots, he explained, go into stews, niharis, and shorbas, where their woody and floral notes need long braising to come through. The stems belong in kadhai preparations and medium-cook dishes. The leaves are reserved for chutneys, marinades, and last-minute garnishes.

> **"Chopping should happen in the last minute before garnishing.

"The cooking time reduces as one graduates from roots to stems to leaves."**

Timing Is Everything

Brar's rule of thumb is straightforward. If a dish will cook for two to three hours — a slow-braised curry, a nihari, a rich gravy — add the stems early. If the dish takes 15 to 20 minutes or needs a fresh finish, use the leaves, and add them at the very last moment.

The reason is chemistry. The flavor molecules in coriander leaves are highly volatile. Brar estimates that cutting the leaves and leaving them out for just one hour causes a loss of roughly 20 percent of the aromatic top notes. Chopping should happen in the last minute before garnishing.

"The cooking time reduces as one graduates from roots to stems to leaves. This is the basic guideline."

— Chef Ranveer Brar
Storing Coriander Right
›Avoid washing coriander before refrigerating.
›Use ziplock bags with a moist tissue.
›Revive wilted coriander in chilled water.
›Moisture causes rapid spoilage.

How to Store It Right

Brar is equally particular about storage. The biggest mistake, he says, is washing fresh coriander immediately after bringing it home and putting it in the fridge while still wet. Moisture causes rapid spoilage.

His method: refrigerate in ziplock bags with a moist tissue tucked inside to prevent drying without adding excess water. When ready to cook, revive wilted coriander by placing it in chilled water — not iced, which bruises the delicate leaves. Chilled water strengthens the herb and restores its springy texture.

A Pantry Staple Worth Rethinking

For Indian households — whether in Mumbai or Minneapolis — coriander is arguably the most frequently used fresh herb. A single bunch typically costs a few rupees at Indian vegetable markets and is sometimes given free with other purchases. Yet the stems, which carry the bulk of its value, end up in the compost bin.

Brar's advice applies beyond Indian cooking. Coriander stems hold up well in Thai curries, Mexican salsas, and Southeast Asian soups — any dish where extended cooking can extract their woody depth. The next time a recipe calls for a handful of chopped coriander, consider what you might be throwing away.
